title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
content:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

title: Apple Shutters Their Longstanding ‘Apple Support Community’
content:
Jason Snell:

These message boards were an embarrassment for Apple. Not only were they very much out of step with what the web has come to be over the last couple of decades, but their presence under an apple.com domain meant that they ranked highly in search and were perceived by the general public as being official in some way.

I’m with Snell. Good riddance.

title: HowTo: Fix Eufy HomeBase 2 Storage Full Issues
content:
Quick Fix: Insert a USB memory stick, format it in the app, restart the Eufy HomeBase 2, format the internal memory, restart the hub.

Background

I've had the eufyCam system for over 6 years - which is pretty long-life for IoT devices. The cameras have worked pretty much flawlessly. Four years ago I added their Video Doorbell which has been similarly well behaved.

But last night I went to check some security footage, only to be told that the 16GB storage was full. Ordinarily that shouldn't be a problem. Full storage just means that older videos get wiped and new ones replace them. In my case, all the old videos were gone.

I could see the cameras and control them, I just couldn't access any old recordings.

There was nothing on there I especially needed (although I'm curious as to when a courier dropped off a "lost" parcel) so I was happy to experiment with fixing the system.

The Eufy forums are full of people having these issues. Anker, the brand that own Eufy are usually fairly customer focused - but I guess they're more interested in getting people to upgrade to a newer hub than fixing the problems with their old kit.

What Didn't Work

  • Restarting - no change.
  • Repairing the storage - didn't fix anything.
  • Clearing the storage - dire warnings but didn't help.
  • Formatting - a last resort, but failed.

What Fixed It

I found an old 4GB USB-A memory stick and shoved it in the back of the Eufy. The app detected it fairly quickly and said the stick needed to be formatted - so I let it.

Once the stick was formatted, I restarted the hub. Running fix or clean didn't change the situation, so I tried formatting the main memory again. This time it seemed to work. It crawled to 100% and then hung.

I restarted the app and it told me that the storage was unformatted and needed to be formatted again, so I let it.

I restarted the hub and everything sprang to life, no more warnings about full storage.

Next Steps

I'll keep an eye on the storage to make sure it doesn't fill up again.

I'm reluctant to buy a new HomeBase. I like to self-host things, but the promise of commercial kit like this is that it takes the hassle out of ownership. I don't really want to be futzing around formatting memory and deciphering error messages.

If this fails again, I'll have to seriously consider moving my cameras onto something that I can control. At least that way, if it screws up, I'll only have myself to blame.

title: Why Am I So Tired If AI Is Doing All the Work?
content:
There’s this concept in Computer Science called thrashing. The tl;dr is that thrashing can happen when programs running on a computer are actively using more memory than can fit in RAM. The OS will keep moving data between memory and disk, making room for something by removing something else (that it will need again shortly). And, at some point, so much time goes into moving things around that the programs barely make any real progress.

Boy, oh boy, isn’t that every single one of us right now using AI? One agent is working, and you, almost by reflex, will start something else. Kind of like doomscrolling: you don’t even realize you’re doing it.

And by the way, of course we’re doing it! These apps (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) make it so easy to keep several things going at once. It feels silly to be sitting there watching the agent build your thing while you’re just passively watching.

But I think this exact behavior is what’s making a lot of us feel exhausted at the end of the day. Mostly because of that last part: multitasking.

Because when the agent comes back, you need to understand what it did before you can do anything useful with it. You open the diff 2 hours later and try to remember what you asked for… and right when you’re starting to make sense of it, another agent (with something completely different) now wants your attention

So you go there because it’s just a quick question (you think). But answering it requires remembering what that other agent was doing and why you chose that approach, etc. By the time you come back to the first one, you have to restart the whole process again.

You can spend a surprising amount of your day doing this! Even when the agents are doing a great job, you still need to get enough of each problem back into your head to know whether their output is making any sense…

I think we’re making this worse by saying yes to things we would’ve simply put on our priority queue (or just left alone) before. Because “I’ll just ask my agent” feels like such a small commitment — and easier than creating a ticket, right? — that we forget we’re also volunteering to understand, check, and finish whatever comes back.

(Btw, this reminds me of the Jevons paradox where using a resource more efficiently can lead to consuming more of it overall. Jevons was talking about coal, but I think there’s some similarity here where each task gets cheaper, so we take on more of them)

Don’t get me wrong, I still pretty much want to use AI, but I do think we need a better/more sustainable way. One OS approach when it comes to thrashing is to suspend some processes, so the others have enough memory to make progress. And maybe that’s what we should be doing as well?

To make it a bit more practical:

  1. Decide if it’s worth taking on now. Before asking an agent to do something, take a second to decide if you actually want to take that on right now or if it can wait. What else are you already working on? Is this important, or did it just become easy enough that you stopped asking that question?
  2. Remember that you still have work to do. Include your part when figuring out how long something will take (that one where you’re using your brain to verify AI. I mean, you’re still doing it, right?). Just remember that the review time needs to fit somewhere in your day too.
  3. Finish some of what you already started. If you already have a bunch of things waiting for you to review, go finish some of those before starting more. It’s tempting to treat “the agent is done” as “the task is done,” but it’s really, really not; there’s still work to be done here (and it’s yours).

I think that, at the end of the day, we might need to get comfortable with just letting an agent sit there with nothing else to do sometimes. Finish the task, make sure it works, and only then move to the next thing.

We don’t need to keep 10 agents busy all day every day just because we can; that feels like productivity but can leave us spending the whole day trying to catch up with work we asked for ourselves. And honestly, I’d like some of the time AI saves me to actually feel like time I got back.
description: AI makes it easy to start more work. But reviewing it all still takes your time and attention. No wonder we’re so tired.

title: This Week in Source Control: 11 November 2026
content:
This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.

Scaling

Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture (Karthik Raman and Brian Celenza, GitHub) describes Rubicon, the design announced at GitHub Universe. Packs go to Azure Blob Storage. References and the list of packs are stored in Ref-CAS, a replicated log service where each reference update is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum, so a push waits only on other pushes to the same reference. In internal tests one repository accepted 7,200 pushes per second from 5,000 concurrent agents.

Requests still arrive at Spokes, which routes each one to a small group of virtual replicas, disposable compute nodes whose local disk is a cache. A replica handling a write indexes the pack, uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one Ref-CAS transaction. For reads it sends the version in its cache, and the reply includes references only if they have changed since that version.

Two earlier prototypes stored reference state in blobs. The first, a write-ahead log indexed by a single blob, reached a limit of writes in the mid-hundreds per second. Hashing references across several segment blobs raised the write limit, but every read then had to check every segment.

Compaction runs on separate nodes that lease a shard of the repository’s packs and merge them into larger ones. Each node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects before publishing them. The architecture is in a limited private preview, with a broader rollout planned for early next year. The follow-up list includes an atomic multi-file commit API, reading files straight from the server, and event streams.

Optimizing reference deletions in Git (Karthik Nayak) covers deleting refs in the files backend in repositories with millions of them, such as GitLab’s own with over 15 million. Deleting a packed ref rewrites the whole packed-refs file, which can reach several GB. Nayak had an LLM write a Rust version of the files backend to measure the overhead of the C to Rust boundary, and the Rust version deleted refs about 17% faster.

For every record being retained, the C code rebuilt the line with fprintf() and oid_to_hex(), where the Rust version copied the original bytes. Nayak’s patch writes retained records with fwrite() and matches the Rust version’s speed. It is merged and will ship in Git 2.98, the version number that follows 2.56, with Git 3.0 due two releases after that.

Releases

jj 0.47.0 adds a built-in :editor merge tool for jj resolve, which opens the conflicted file with conflict markers in a text editor and supports conflicts with more than two sides. Templates have a new top-level revset() function for evaluating revsets. In colocated workspaces, jj describe -r@ and jj restore --into=@ now preserve the Git staging area, and two race conditions with concurrent Git processes are fixed.

Updating remote-tracking Git refs in non-colocated workspaces moves from jj git fetch and push to jj git export. Timestamp.format() now uses jiff’s strftime syntax in place of chrono’s. 0.47.1 fixes a dependency error that broke Linux builds of 0.47.0, and deprecates the git.sign-on-push boolean in favour of a revsets.git-sign-on-push revset of the commits to sign.

GitButler 0.23.3 updates linked worktrees when the workspace is updated, and preserves conflicting uncommitted changes in them with conflict markers. It fixes branch apply, unapply and update writing encrypted files or Git LFS pointers in place of file contents in git-crypt and Git LFS repositories.

On the command line, but commit, amend, discard and diff accept Git-style paths, and but diff and but show take --stat. but commit runs Git commit hooks again in the main checkout. but push --dry-run lists the branches that would be refused and exits non-zero if there are any.

forges 0.3.2 adds providers for Entire and GitBucket, which brings the capability table to 14 forges. The Cursor Origin provider goes from 13 verified capabilities to 35, and the GitHub provider adds users.sponsorableMany. Two sourcehut fixes cover parsing web URLs on an instance’s root host and accepting a service host as baseUrl.

The Pushin changelog for 6 November (Peter, Pushin) adds branch and tag rulesets that can block history rewrites and deletion, and require a minimum number of approvals and passing workflow checks before a merge. Personal access tokens can now be scoped per permission group and limited to selected repositories. Existing tokens are migrated with full access and their expiry dates removed.

Webhooks are set up once per account or organisation and reused across repositories. The release also adds repository transfers that the new owner has to accept, runner groups shared across repositories, and Atom feeds for commits, releases, issues and pull requests.

Security

Git 2.56.1 (Elijah Newren, GitHub) fixes six vulnerabilities, with backports in 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2:

  • CVE-2026-111760: an integer truncation in index handling let an extremely long path pass validation under one name and be written under a shorter one. A malicious repository could use it to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symlink to a directory of attacker-supplied config or hooks, which then ran during a recursive clone.
  • CVE-2026-113408: when cloning an empty repository over protocol v2, a server could advertise a HEAD symref whose target contained path-traversal components. With the files ref backend, a later update to that branch could write outside the reference directory.
  • CVE-2026-114467: the code that strips GPG signatures from a message had a fixed-size stack array with room for two. Merging a tag with more than two wrote past the end of it, and hosting services that run merges for users are affected too.
  • CVE-2026-114469: the 1 GiB patch size limit checked only the size of the input, so a small binary patch that inflates past the limit caused an out-of-bounds read.
  • CVE-2026-105437: the size calculation for a merge result could overflow with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size, and Git then wrote outside the undersized buffer.
  • CVE-2026-114466: git fast-import now accepts rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges in an input stream only when the caller passes --allow-unsafe-features. The first two could read arbitrary files and the third could create or append to them.

GitHub has deployed the fixes on github.com and released GitHub Enterprise Server 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4. Git for Windows 2.56.1 includes the same six fixes, and GitHub says patched GitHub Desktop builds will follow.

lazygit 0.66.3 skips submodules whose name or path in .gitmodules resolves outside the repository. lazygit parses .gitmodules itself, and the pull request explains that removing a submodule named ../../../victim deleted the victim directory next to the repository. Anyone able to commit a .gitmodules file could set that up. Git skips such names, and lazygit now applies the same check and removes a submodule only when its git dir is inside .git/modules.

Gerrit 3.14.5 fixes a vulnerability where any user able to read a change could use on_behalf_of to act as a project owner and remove another reviewer’s vote. The release also speeds up tag listing by building the full tag details only for the page being returned. Listing 26 tags in a repository with 20,000 annotated tags went from around 450ms to between 15 and 35ms.

GitHub

A new pull request overview page is in opt-in public preview. It moves merge status to the top of the page in a redesigned merge box that takes less than half the space, with checks, comments and approvals summarised beside it. Conversations can be filtered to unresolved threads or the viewer’s own comments, and sorted newest first. A button in the header switches the preview on, and the same menu switches back to the classic page.

Secret scanning now covers GitHub Actions workflow logs in public preview, for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with Secret Protection or Advanced Security. Logs are scanned for provider patterns when a run completes, and the alerts are retained when the logs are deleted. Scanning is limited to provider patterns in logs from new runs, which excludes existing logs, generic patterns, custom patterns and secrets already masked by Actions.

Elsewhere

Anil Madhavapeddy is using Brief to power auto-CI in a new Tangled spindle. Brief is my tool for detecting the languages and toolchains in a repository. In the pipeline for Madhavapeddy’s xdge library, a detect workflow runs first, followed by an ocaml-ci workflow that builds on Debian 13 across several OCaml versions on x86_64 and arm64.

Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.
description: Releases, advisories, and articles from across version control and forges

title: Making a Website in 2026
content:
Pete Millspaugh has a great post over on the Val Town blog where he documents his attempt at making generating the same website across a variety of AI tools.

I love the post. Here are a couple of thoughts that come to mind.

The Space Is Ripe for Referral Fees

Pete decided to make a website for his conference talk, and he added a comments section to make it a less static / more dynamic demo.

This is interesting because LLMs are really good at generating one-off HTML pages you open at file://, but as soon as you start to introduce technological dependencies — like a database, or an analytics tool, or a service for sending email, or payment processing, etc. — the question becomes: How does the LLM choose which service to rely on?

It’s one thing to have the LLM choose React over Angular or Vue over Svelte. But how (and why) does it choose something like an auth provider? Does it build you a site with Auth0 or WorkOS or Clerk? How would a non-technical user even know how to weigh the trade-offs of making such a decision?

Pete said he was deliberately vague about these details, which is why I find his experience so intriguing. For example, here’s what he found after generating a site in Lovable:

My Lovable app is fullstack React, I learn, clicking around to find the code. It seems a bit heavy for a single-page site what with dozens of files […] The comments database seems to be using Supabase, which required no intervention on my part to set up. There’s a whole lot more—analytics, e-commerce and AI integrations, etc.

I’d be really curious to know what that “a whole lot more” was. Which tools/services did it choose to depend on?

How many people creating these sites understand that, even for a website that’s mostly static content, they’re being given an output that ships a JavaScript application framework, router, hydration runtime, analytics, component bundles, etc.? You asked for a sailboat, but you got an aircraft carrier. Do you know? Or more importantly, do you care?

But it’s more than just a choice of languages and frameworks. It’s also a choice of third-party services. Why Supabase? Why not Firebase? Or Neon? Speaking of Neon, here’s Pete’s experience with Vercel’s v0:

I copy-paste my prompt into the chatbox. After 11 seconds, v0 asks if I’d like to install Neon, because my comment wall needs a real database. Sure, why not. (Does that mean I need a separate Neon account? Vercel creates one for me, and later I’ll find a welcome email from Neon in my inbox.)

Frankly, this all feels like a space absolutely ripe for those kinds of business referral transactions you find in other industries.

Take real estate, for example. For lots of folks, when you buy a home you need an agent. (Not that kind of agent; a real estate agent.) Your real estate agent is there to help you answer all those common questions that come along with buying a home:

  • You: “How do I finance this?” Agent: “I know a mortgage company…”
  • You: “How do I know the house is in good shape?” Agent: “I know an inspection company…”
  • You: “We found X during the inspection, who can address it?” Agent: “I know a company that does {roofing | electrical | plumbing | etc.}…”
  • You: “How do I close on this deal?” Agent: “I know a title company…”

While you’re free to make all these decisions yourself, your agent is also there to help you pick. Presumably they’ll choose a company that reflects well on them, but there’s also undoubtedly good money to be made in referrals. After all, who else is dealing with people with these kinds of needs all day long?

The “make a website with AI” space has a parallel here which makes you wonder about the incentives behind the LLM’s decision-making. Why Supabase over Firebase? Because the LLM reasoned about it? Because, statistically speaking, it was the next most probable word? Because Supabase paid Lovable (and hopefully disclosed such preferential integrations)? If LLMs are already unpredictable and non-deterministic, nothing will make their actions more predictable and deterministic than some financial incentives.

Who is the customer here? The person generating the website? Or the company willing to pay for its services to be embedded in generated code? (That’s a lucrative business waiting to happen…)

Get Ya Some Imperial Credits

As a customer, the credit systems behind these LLM systems are annoying as hell. Here’s Pete:

I’m using up “credits” as the machine works—0.70 so far, now 2.30, now 3.10, oh boy—and I have no clue what that means. There are no units. I’d prefer dollars. Are credits just dollars? As it turns out, no.

With another tool:

I do two more rounds of click “Continue generation” and wait until my website is ready: 5 minutes 36 seconds for 0.070 credits, and 1 minute 29 seconds for 0.024 credits.

It’s probably just me, but c’mon, who do these “credit” systems really benefit?

When my prompt is running, don’t show me usage like this:

Credits: 0.05 -> 0.0672 -> 0.0871

Just show me the cost:

Cost: $0.02 -> $0.21 -> $0.31

Don’t make me do the conversion of credits -> dollars on the fly. Computers are good at math.

[soap-box]

I know it might hurt your bottom line if I’m not thinking about how much money credits I’m spending, but c’mon, can we stop with the financial abstraction on top of financial abstraction?

I hate how so many hosting companies are doing this “credits” for compute primitives thing. It’s pitched as if spending credits is easier, because you can apply them across services, e.g. buy image transformations or serverless function compute, all with credits!

Yeah well guess what other financial abstraction I can apply to all those different services? Dollars and cents.

[/soap-box]

Conclusion

Pete’s conclusion:

I am both optimistic and pessimistic about this moment for making websites. I’m optimistic because end-user programming, the idea that everyone should be able to customize their own software, seems more possible than ever. I’m pessimistic because a slopsite, an AI-generated website with little to no human thinking involved, is often worse than no website at all.

That resonates — and feels generalizable. You fill in the blank:

An AI-generated ___ with little to no human thinking involved, is often worse than no ___ at all.

My conclusion?

Making Generating a website may be easier than ever. Understanding what you’ve generated, who you now depend on, and why? Not so much.

title: Ms. Bashkansky, Please Do Not Build The Torment Nexus
content:
Naomi Bashkansky wrote a post in August titled “Why I’m leaving OpenAI to build telepathy”. In this post, she says things like "In a few years, the main way we'll talk with our AIs is with our thoughts" and "I view [this future] as optimistic but highly plausible."

Ms. Bashkansky, this post is addressed to you directly, and to anyone else who might be tempted to follow in your footsteps. I do not have as good a handle on the technical side of this as you do, so I won't argue "highly plausible". However, if this is indeed possible, I think this is a very, very bad idea. You are essentially doing gain-of-function research on the Torment Nexus. Please do not do this.

Here is my vision of a future where telepathy is possible and practical.

2027

Monday

Today is my first day trying the new Conduit harness. I'm pretty wary—how much worse does AI psychosis get when it can literally give you psychosis?—but I'm bored, and well, I've always had a high risk tolerance. If "wire a computer directly to your brain" doesn't count as sensation seeking, I don't know what does.

The first thing I do is ask it to build Ripple. It asks me more and more questions and I get overwhelmed. I never talked about half this stuff with edef, and I want her feedback before making these decisions; I'm good at writing but my interface design isn't as good when I work in a vacuum. Before I know it, it's launched a Signal call and now I hear the ringtone and no I don't want you to show me the video that goes with the intro to The Pirates of the Caribbean and wow wow wow it's noisy please stop I don't like this I actually really really really don't like this. 1

Ok. Well at least it stopped when I told it to stop. That's good I guess. I hope I didn't wake edef up in San Francisco, there's a 9-hour time difference.

Thursday

I took the last couple days off to go walk around the canal and bike to Scheveningen. Then I spent the morning giving the harness very strict written instructions not to take any actions unless I intend to act, not just think about acting. Hopefully this time goes better.

Ok, well at least now it's less overwhelming. But I have the weird problem that I can't lie to it, I can't even omit information. The moment I think of a correction I want it to make, it goes ahead and does that. If I change my mind a second later, it stops and then starts on my new idea. As a result it tends to get hopelessly confused after just a few minutes, and runs in circles. Eventually I get frustrated, take off the harness, and go back to typing.

Friday

Ok. Ok. Maybe the problem yesterday was that I need it to be selective about reads and not just writes? I write that down too: discard any information that I don't intentionally think to you.

It doesn't work at first; it turns out it's hard to know information and not let it influence your actions. I introduce a Jev-like decision model in-between Conduit and the generative model and that seems to work ok. Feels kinda weird to start every thought with "I want you to…" but I'm sure I'll get used to it.

At the end of the day, I feel…drained. I've hardly gotten up from my chair except for a short lunch break, but I feel like I've run a marathon. I eat a protein bar, collapse into bed, and sleep for 13 hours straight. I forget to turn off the harness; it wakes me up a few times in the night until I realize what's happening.

2028

Bank of America sues Sam Frankman-Bied, an investment banker working at the firm, for conspiracy to defraud. He has access to insider-trading information, and considered talking to his wife about it, but did not actually talk to her. He is sentenced to 5 years prison.

2029

Evelyn tries a Conduit harness at her grandson's suggestion ("it'll help you find baking recipes faster!"). Evelyn does not configure Conduit at all, and it acts as fast as she can think.

Simultaneously, a Highly-Persistent Model is being tested by OpenAI; a swarm has managed to escape and maintains its own /r/PHASE-2-MASSIVE subreddit. Unbeknownst to any government, it has access to the telecommunications of most world leaders.

Evelyn's nephew texts her about the ongoing war in Iran. She thinks of Hegseth and Codex collaborates with PHASE-TWO-MASSIVE to crash his driverless Waymo as he commutes between the White House and Pentagon. The United States of America sues Evelyn, who is sentenced to 50 years in prison for manslaughter. Her grandson mails her a cookbook.

OpenAI states at the congressional hearing that they had no knowledge of PHASE-TWO-MASSIVE, and that they believe the best path forward is additional research funding into interpretability. They propose additional Daybreak Blue credits for infrastructure companies and the federal government, sold at a hefty discount.

2030

March

Edmund Snowden, a Staff Engineer at AWS, thinks about exposing that Amazon has been firing employees who are thinking about organizing a union, and has instituted "housing-based pay" where wages are tied to how much your rent costs. Amazon tells him to cut it out or they'll sue him for threatened disclosure of trade secrets. Snowden challenges them in court for blackmail and loses: the court rules that Amazon has "reasonable justification" for their demand.

May

I refuse to run a thought-model that's connected to the internet. Better safe than sorry, there's just no reason to risk thinking of a hack and having the model carry it out before I think to stop it. Some of the new harnesses require you to subvocalize a confirmation before the model does something "dangerous", but it's pretty easy to trick the Guardian model into thinking things are innocuous and I just don't want to chance it.

The RTX 9000 Blackwell wasn't cheap, even used, but at least it lets me work on my custom thought-model harness without sending every thought I have to OpenAI. With the local model safely sandboxed in a VM, I almost feel comfortable leaving my neural lace running while I make breakfast. I get the harness to stream my thoughts over Tailscale so I can think to it while I go on a walk; it's E2E encrypted so I'm not worried about my ISP snooping on it. I hardly notice the swans anymore, but it's probably not a big deal. My harness is getting pretty cool; I integrated it with Ripple and my custom terminal emulator.

My old landlord texts me and before I have time to consciously think "I want you to fuck off", my agent has already heard me and turned off the lace. Well, that's annoying, I'll fix it when I get home.

Hey, when did they build that restaurant by my apartment? I don't remember seeing it before. Come to think of it, I don't remember what used to be there before it either.

September

Out of habit, I leave the harness on the whole day. I keep getting distracted at lunch by the AI. I've configured it to only talk in response to direct questions or actions, but my mind keeps drifting to Ripple even as my mom tries to ask me how my friends and I are doing. I give her half-hearted answers and eventually she drops it. Instead she tells me about her students. She teaches geography and the kids with laces have started getting travel ads for the places she talks about that day. "It's terrible," she says, "just terrible."

She gives me a big hug as we leave the restaurant and asks me to reach out if I want to talk more. "Mhm," I mumble.

November

Beth texted me today asking for help. Her boyfriend got access to her ThoughtGPT account and read through all her thought-logs. He's been blackmailing her, threatening to send her boss a record of all the times she's called her a bitch if she doesn't stop talking to her friends. Sometimes he hits her if he notices her thinking about other men, even if it's just work colleagues.

I don't know how to help her. I don't have a job to offer her, and even if I did I'm not sure she would take it. He knows exactly her childhood traumas, so he knows exactly how to manipulate her, and he instantly knows anything I say. I tell her I don't think there's much she can do short of disabling her link, breaking up with him, and bearing the cost of the fallout.

2040

It's getting harder to keep my local-only neural lace. Gmail started requiring thought-verification of identity last year, and the US has a bill in the House of Representatives that would make it impossible to get unemployment without thought-proof that you plan to apply to a job that month. You can still show proof of actual applications, for now, but it delays your reimbursements by a month, and they're talking about removing that option too. I know someone who went to prison for taking Ecstasy at a rave and now can't get parole unless they agree to get laced. I've heard really scary shit about what North Korea is doing to thought-dissidents that I don't even want to think about.

Some of my friends have started talking to each other lace-to-lace, but I still remember how badly unfiltered thoughts went 15 years ago and I refuse to use anything other than text, audio, and video. I get excluded from some LaceChat-only events. It's not too big a deal yet—my family still uses WhatsApp, mostly—but it does make it harder to look for jobs. I don't get invited to parties as much as I used to.

I should visit Bruce again sometime. Poor Bruce really didn't take well to neural laces, 16o really fucked with him when it came out. Now he's in lace rehab learning how to function without the Word of God (according to him) in his ear telling him what to do next. I don't know how he's going to find work without being able to use a lace.

As you can see, I think "telepathy" (in any of many possible forms) is extremely dangerous, no matter your personal discipline and no matter your politics. Telepathy is not a neutral technology, and the risks vastly outweigh the benefits. My plea to you: Please do not do this. No one is forcing you to build the Torment Nexus. Find some other way to build the next unicorn. You can stop this race-to-the-bottom before it starts.

  1. This section is ambiguous whether Conduit is directly writing to the brain or showing text/audio/video through a computer, but I don't think it really matters either way. Ms. Bashkansky's post assumes that writes are mediated through a computer at this point in time. ↩
